title: Thai Green Curry Recipe
text:
# Thai Green Curry Recipe

A fragrant dish I first tried at a street stall in Bangkok. The aroma of lemongrass and galangal took me right back to that humid evening wandering through Chinatown.

## Ingredients

- 400ml coconut milk
- 2 tbsp green curry paste
- 300g chicken thigh, sliced
- 1 stalk lemongrass, bruised
- 3 kaffir lime leaves
- 1 tbsp fish sauce
- 1 tsp palm sugar
- Thai basil leaves
- 2 Japanese eggplants, sliced
- Handful of bamboo shoots

## Method

Heat a splash of coconut cream in a wok until it splits. Fry the curry paste for two minutes until aromatic. Add the chicken pieces and cook until sealed on all sides. Pour in the remaining coconut milk along with the lemongrass, lime leaves, fish sauce, and palm sugar. Simmer for fifteen minutes.

Add the eggplant and bamboo shoots. Cook for another five minutes until the vegetables are tender. Finish with torn Thai basil.

## Tips

The key to authentic flavor is using fresh paste rather than jarred. If you can find galangal at an Asian grocery, it makes a noticeable difference. Toast whole spices like coriander seeds and cumin before grinding them into the paste.

Serve over jasmine rice. This feeds four people comfortably and the leftovers taste even better the next day as the spices develop overnight.

title: Sourdough Bread Baking
text:
# Sourdough Bread Baking

My weekend ritual. There is something meditative about the slow fermentation process — feeding the starter Friday night, mixing Saturday morning, baking Saturday afternoon.

## The Starter

A sourdough starter is a living culture of wild yeast and lactobacilli. Mine is three years old now. Feed it equal parts flour and water by weight every day if kept at room temperature, or once a week if refrigerated. A healthy starter should double in volume within 4-6 hours after feeding.

## Basic Formula

- 500g bread flour
- 350g water (70% hydration)
- 100g active starter
- 10g salt

Mix flour and water, let it autolyse for 30 minutes. Add starter and salt, then do stretch-and-folds every 30 minutes for the first two hours. Bulk fermentation takes 4-6 hours at room temperature depending on ambient temperature.

## Shaping and Baking

Pre-shape into a round, rest 20 minutes, then final shape into a batard or boule. Place seam-side up in a floured banneton. Cold retard in the refrigerator overnight for deeper flavor development.

Bake in a preheated Dutch oven at 250C with the lid on for 20 minutes, then remove lid and bake at 230C for another 20-25 minutes until the crust is deeply caramelized.

## Troubleshooting

Dense crumb usually means under-fermentation. Gummy interior means the loaf needed more time in the oven. If the crust is too thick, try adding steam to the oven or reducing the bake time slightly.

title: Meal Prep for Busy Weeks
text:
# Meal Prep for Busy Weeks

Batch cooking on Sundays saves both time and money during the week. I have been doing this consistently for about six months and my grocery expenditure has dropped noticeably.

## Budget-Friendly Strategy

The key is buying ingredients that overlap across multiple dishes. A bulk purchase of chicken thighs, rice, and seasonal vegetables can form the base of three to four different meals. I typically spend around thirty dollars for a full week of lunches.

Cost-effective protein sources: chicken thighs, canned beans, eggs, tofu. Avoid pre-cut or pre-marinated options — you pay a premium for convenience that takes five minutes to do yourself.

## My Rotation

1. **Monday-Tuesday:** Grain bowls with roasted vegetables and tahini dressing
2. **Wednesday-Thursday:** Stir-fry with whatever protein is on sale
3. **Friday:** Soup or curry from leftover vegetables

## Container System

Glass containers with snap lids last longer than plastic and do not stain. I use 750ml containers for main meals and 250ml ones for snacks. Label everything with masking tape and a marker — date and contents.

## Time Investment

About two hours on Sunday covers the entire week. Prep all vegetables first, then cook grains and proteins in parallel. The oven does most of the work while you handle stovetop items.

title: Japanese Knife Skills
text:
# Japanese Knife Skills

After taking a workshop in Kyoto, I became fascinated with the precision of Japanese blade work. The instructor said that a sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it goes where you direct it.

## Types of Japanese Knives

- **Gyuto:** The Japanese equivalent of a Western chef's knife. Lighter and thinner.
- **Santoku:** All-purpose knife with a flatter profile. Great for vegetables.
- **Nakiri:** Double-bevel vegetable knife. Perfect for precise julienne cuts.
- **Petty:** Small utility knife for detailed work.

## Honing and Sharpening

Japanese knives use harder steel (typically 60-67 HRC on the Rockwell scale) than Western knives. This means they hold an edge longer but require more careful maintenance.

Use a whetstone rather than a honing steel. Start with a 1000-grit stone for regular sharpening and finish with a 3000-grit or higher for polishing the edge. Soak the stone in water for fifteen minutes before use.

Maintain a consistent angle of 15 degrees on each side. Draw the blade across the stone in smooth, even strokes. Ten to fifteen passes per side is usually sufficient for routine maintenance.

## Care Tips

Never put Japanese knives in the dishwasher. Hand wash and dry immediately after use. Store on a magnetic strip or in a knife roll — never loose in a drawer where edges can chip against other utensils.

title: Fermented Foods Guide
text:
# Fermented Foods Guide

Fermentation is one of the oldest methods of food preservation. Cultures around the world have developed their own traditions — Korean kimchi, German sauerkraut, Japanese miso, Eastern European kefir.

## The Science

Lactic acid fermentation occurs when beneficial bacteria (primarily Lactobacillus) convert sugars into lactic acid in an anaerobic environment. This lowers the pH, creating conditions hostile to harmful pathogens while developing complex flavors.

The process also increases bioavailability of nutrients and produces probiotics that support gut health. Studies suggest regular consumption of cultured foods may improve digestion and immune function.

## Getting Started with Sauerkraut

The simplest fermented food to make at home. Shred one head of cabbage, toss with two tablespoons of salt, and massage until liquid is released. Pack tightly into a jar, making sure the brine covers the cabbage. Weight it down and cover loosely.

Ferment at room temperature for one to four weeks, tasting periodically. The flavor shifts from salty to tangy as the bacteria do their work. Refrigerate once it reaches your preferred taste — cold temperatures slow the culturing process dramatically.

## Beyond Sauerkraut

Once comfortable with basic vegetable ferments, try kombucha (fermented tea), water kefir, or hot sauce. Each uses the same fundamental principle of creating conditions for beneficial microorganisms to thrive while keeping harmful ones at bay.

title: Budget Backpacking Southeast Asia
text:
# Budget Backpacking Southeast Asia

Three months across Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos for under four thousand dollars total. Here is how I kept costs down without sacrificing the experience.

## Accommodation

Hostel dorm beds range from four to ten dollars per night depending on the city. In smaller towns, guesthouses are often cheaper than hostels and include a private room. Always negotiate rates for stays longer than three nights — most owners will offer a discount.

## Food Costs

Street food is both the cheapest and the most delicious option. A bowl of pho in Hanoi costs about one dollar fifty. Pad thai from a Bangkok street vendor is around two dollars. Night markets in Chiang Mai offer incredible variety for under three dollars per meal.

Avoid tourist-oriented restaurants near major attractions. Walk two blocks in any direction and prices drop by half. Local markets where residents actually shop have the best prices and freshest ingredients.

## Transportation

Overnight buses and trains save on accommodation costs. The Bangkok to Chiang Mai sleeper train is about fifteen dollars for a second-class berth. Grab and local ride-hailing apps are cheaper than taxis everywhere.

## Daily Budget Breakdown

- Accommodation: $6-8
- Food: $8-12
- Transport: $3-5
- Activities: $5-10
- **Total: $22-35 per day**

The biggest expense trap is organized tours. Many activities — temple visits, hiking, waterfall trips — can be done independently for a fraction of the cost.

title: Hiking the Pacific Crest Trail
text:
# Hiking the Pacific Crest Trail

Section-hiked the Oregon portion last summer. 455 miles from the California border to the Columbia River Gorge. Took about three weeks at a comfortable pace.

## Gear List

Lightweight backpacking makes long-distance hiking sustainable. My base weight was twelve pounds.

### Big Three

- **Shelter:** Zpacks Duplex (19 oz) — expensive but worth every penny for a thru-hike
- **Pack:** ULA Circuit (39 oz) — comfortable with loads up to 30 lbs
- **Sleep system:** Enlightened Equipment quilt 20F (22 oz) + Thermarest NeoAir XLite (12 oz)

### Clothing

Merino wool base layer, wind shirt, lightweight rain jacket, running shorts, sun hoody. Two pairs of Darn Tough socks on rotation. Trail runners instead of boots — faster drying and lighter.

### Navigation and Safety

Guthook app (now FarOut) for trail navigation and water source beta. InReach Mini for emergency communication. Small first aid kit focused on blister care and ibuprofen.

## Trail Conditions

Oregon PCT is relatively gentle compared to the Sierra or Washington sections. Well-maintained trail with good signage. Water sources are reliable through July but some creeks dry up by late August.

Mosquito season peaks in July around the lake regions. Bring a head net and treat clothing with permethrin before departure.

## Resupply Strategy

Mailed resupply boxes to Crater Lake, Shelter Cove, Big Lake Youth Camp, and Timberline Lodge. Supplement with grocery stops in Bend and Cascade Locks.

title: Tokyo Food Markets
text:
# Tokyo Food Markets

Tokyo's market scene is an education in quality and presentation. Every visit teaches me something new about ingredient selection and culinary craftsmanship.

## Tsukiji Outer Market

The inner wholesale market moved to Toyosu, but the outer market remains a vibrant destination. Arrive before 8 AM for the best experience. Vendors sell everything from dried bonito to specialty knives to fresh tamago (egg omelet) on sticks.

Stand-up sushi counters here serve some of the freshest fish in Tokyo at reasonable prices. A chef's choice plate of eight pieces runs about 2500 yen — roughly twenty dollars for quality you would pay triple for elsewhere.

## Depachika (Department Store Basements)

The food halls beneath Japanese department stores are extraordinary. Isetan Shinjuku and Mitsukoshi Ginza have the most impressive selections. Wagashi (traditional sweets), bento boxes assembled with surgical precision, and seasonal fruits displayed like jewelry.

The prices can be steep — a single mango might cost thirty dollars — but the quality justifies the expense for special occasions. Late evening visits (after 7 PM) often yield discounted items as vendors prepare to close.

## Ameya-Yokocho (Ameyoko)

The street market near Ueno station is the opposite of depachika elegance. Chaotic, loud, and full of bargains. Dried seafood, spices, and snacks sold by weight. This is where locals go for affordable ingredients rather than tourist souvenirs.

title: Road Trip Planning Checklist
text:
# Road Trip Planning Checklist

After several cross-country drives, I have developed a system for planning that minimizes stress and keeps fuel expenses manageable.

## Vehicle Preparation

- Check oil level and tire pressure (including spare)
- Inspect brake pads and windshield wipers
- Top off all fluids: coolant, washer fluid, transmission
- Verify registration and insurance documents are current
- Pack a basic emergency kit: jumper cables, flashlight, first aid

## Route Optimization

Use GasBuddy to identify the cheapest fuel stops along your route. Plan refueling at quarter-tank rather than waiting until near-empty — you get better prices when you can be selective about stations.

Avoid toll roads when the time difference is less than fifteen minutes. The cumulative toll expense on a multi-day trip adds up quickly. Google Maps lets you toggle toll avoidance in routing preferences.

## Packing Efficiency

Pack a cooler with drinks and snacks to reduce convenience store stops. Each gas station snack run averages eight to twelve dollars — that adds up to fifty dollars or more over a week-long trip.

## Driving Schedule

Limit driving to six to eight hours per day. Start early (before 7 AM) to avoid traffic and maximize daylight. Schedule a fifteen-minute break every two hours. The most dangerous driving happens when you push past fatigue.

Book accommodation in advance for the first and last nights. Leave middle days flexible for spontaneous detours and discoveries.

title: Digital Nomad Setup in Lisbon
text:
# Digital Nomad Setup in Lisbon

Spent three months working remotely from Lisbon. The city offers an excellent balance of affordable living, reliable internet, and quality of life.

## Coworking Spaces

Second Home LX is the standout — beautiful design, fast wifi, and a great community. Monthly desk is around 250 euros. Outsite Lisbon near the waterfront is more casual and slightly cheaper at 200 euros per month.

Many cafes are laptop-friendly but unreliable for video calls. If your work involves regular meetings, a dedicated coworking membership pays for itself in productivity.

## Living Costs

A furnished apartment in Alfama or Graca runs 800-1200 euros per month. Sharing a flat cuts this to 400-600. Grocery expenses are about 200 euros monthly if you cook at home — significantly cheaper than eating out for every meal.

- Rent: 800-1200 euros
- Coworking: 200-250 euros
- Groceries: 200 euros
- Transport (metro pass): 40 euros
- Eating out (moderate): 150 euros
- **Total: 1400-1840 euros/month**

## Visa and Logistics

Portugal's D7 visa is designed for remote workers and requires proof of stable income (around 760 euros/month minimum). Processing takes two to three months. EU citizens don't need this.

## Productivity Notes

The timezone works well for US East Coast collaboration — six hours ahead means your European morning is free for focused deep work, with meetings starting around 3 PM local time. West Coast overlap is tighter but manageable if you work until 7 PM.

title: Thinking Fast and Slow - Reading Notes
text:
# Thinking, Fast and Slow - Reading Notes

Daniel Kahneman's masterwork on the two systems that drive how we think. This book fundamentally changed how I evaluate my own decision-making.

## System 1 and System 2

System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little effort and no sense of voluntary control. It handles intuitive judgments — recognizing faces, detecting hostility in a voice, driving on an empty road.

System 2 allocates attention to effortful mental activities including complex computations. It is associated with the subjective experience of agency, choice, and concentration.

The critical insight: System 1 continuously generates suggestions for System 2 — impressions, intuitions, intentions, feelings. If endorsed by System 2, impressions turn into beliefs and impulses turn into voluntary actions. System 2 is lazy and often endorses System 1's suggestions with little scrutiny.

## Key Cognitive Biases

- **Anchoring:** Initial exposure to a number influences subsequent estimates, even when the anchor is obviously irrelevant
- **Availability heuristic:** We judge frequency and probability by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual statistics
- **Loss aversion:** Losses loom larger than equivalent gains — losing $100 feels worse than gaining $100 feels good
- **Planning fallacy:** We systematically underestimate time, costs, and risks while overestimating benefits of planned actions

## Practical Applications

Before making important decisions, actively engage System 2. Write down the decision, list alternatives, consider base rates rather than relying on vivid anecdotes. Use pre-mortems: imagine the decision has failed and work backward to identify what went wrong.

title: The Design of Everyday Things - Summary
text:
# The Design of Everyday Things - Summary

Don Norman's argument that good design is invisible. When a product works intuitively, nobody notices the design. When it fails, everyone blames the user — but the fault lies with the designer.

## Core Concepts

### Affordances

An affordance is a relationship between the properties of an object and the capabilities of the agent that determines how the object could possibly be used. A chair affords sitting. A button affords pushing. Good design makes affordances visible and obvious.

### Signifiers

Signifiers communicate where the action should take place. A flat plate on a door signals "push." A handle signals "pull." When signifiers are absent or misleading, people struggle with objects that should be simple.

### Mapping

The relationship between controls and their effects. Natural mapping takes advantage of spatial analogies — a stovetop with burner controls arranged in the same layout as the burners themselves requires no labels.

### Feedback

Every action should produce an immediate, obvious result. A light switch that gives no indication of whether the light is on or off forces the user to look at the ceiling. Good feedback confirms that the system received the input and shows the result.

## The Design Thinking Takeaway

When users make errors, treat it as a design problem, not a user problem. Human error is usually a consequence of poor design — confusing interfaces, unclear controls, missing feedback. The solution is human-centered design that anticipates how real people actually behave, not how designers imagine they should behave.

title: Atomic Habits - Key Takeaways
text:
# Atomic Habits - Key Takeaways

James Clear's framework for building good routines and breaking bad ones. The core thesis: small changes compound into remarkable results over time.

## The Four Laws of Behavior Change

### 1. Make It Obvious

Design your environment so that cues for good habits are visible and cues for bad habits are hidden. If you want to read more, put a book on your pillow. If you want to eat healthier, put fruit on the counter and move junk food to a high shelf.

Habit stacking: link a new habit to an existing one. "After I pour my morning coffee, I will write in my journal for five minutes."

### 2. Make It Attractive

Bundle a habit you need to do with something you enjoy. Listen to your favorite podcast only while exercising. The anticipation of the reward makes the habit more appealing.

### 3. Make It Easy

Reduce friction for good habits and increase friction for bad ones. Lay out gym clothes the night before. Delete social media apps from your phone (you can still access via browser, but the friction reduces mindless scrolling).

The two-minute rule: scale any habit down to something that takes two minutes or less. "Read before bed" becomes "read one page." Once you start, you usually continue.

### 4. Make It Satisfying

Immediate rewards reinforce behavior more effectively than delayed ones. Use a habit tracker — the visual progress of checking off consecutive days creates its own motivation.

## Identity-Based Change

The most powerful shift: focus on who you wish to become, not what you want to achieve. Instead of "I want to run a marathon," think "I am a runner." Each action becomes a vote for your desired identity.

title: Deep Work - Reflections
text:
# Deep Work - Reflections

Cal Newport defines deep work as professional activities performed in a state of distraction-free focus that push your cognitive capabilities to their limit. These efforts create new value, improve your skill, and are hard to replicate.

## The Deep Work Hypothesis

The ability to perform deep work is becoming increasingly rare at exactly the same time it is becoming increasingly valuable in our economy. As a consequence, the few who cultivate this skill will thrive.

Shallow work — logistical-style tasks that can be performed while distracted — is necessary but should be minimized and batched. Email, Slack messages, status meetings: these fill time without producing meaningful output.

## Strategies I Have Adopted

### Time Blocking

Schedule deep work in advance. I block 9 AM to 12 PM every weekday for focused coding or writing. No meetings, no messages, phone on airplane mode. The key is treating these blocks as non-negotiable appointments.

### Shutdown Ritual

At the end of each workday, review incomplete tasks, write tomorrow's plan, and explicitly say "shutdown complete." This creates a clear boundary between work and rest. The ritual trains your brain to release work-related thoughts during off hours.

### Environment Design

A dedicated workspace signals to your brain that it is time to focus. Even small environmental cues help — a specific desk lamp, noise-canceling headphones, or a particular playlist. Consistency in the environment reduces the activation energy needed to enter a flow state.

## Results

Since implementing these practices, my productive output has roughly doubled while my working hours have decreased. The paradox of deep work: doing less but with more intensity produces more than doing many things with divided attention.

title: The Pragmatic Programmer - Notes
text:
# The Pragmatic Programmer - Notes

Hunt and Thomas's classic on software craftsmanship. Written in 1999 but most principles remain timeless. The 20th anniversary edition updated the examples but the core philosophy is unchanged.

## Key Principles

### DRY - Don't Repeat Yourself

Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. Duplication in code is a symptom of a deeper design problem. When you find yourself copying and pasting, stop and extract.

DRY applies beyond code: documentation, database schemas, build scripts, and test fixtures should all have a single source of truth.

### Orthogonality

Components should be self-contained, independent, and have a single well-defined purpose. Changes to one component should not ripple through unrelated parts of the system. Orthogonal designs are easier to test, debug, and modify.

Test for orthogonality: if I dramatically change the requirements behind a particular function, how many modules need to change? In an orthogonal system, the answer is one.

### Tracer Bullets

Build end-to-end thin slices of functionality. Rather than building all layers of a feature before connecting them, create a minimal path from input to output. This gives you a working skeleton to iterate on and validates your architecture early.

## The Broken Window Theory

Don't leave broken windows — bad designs, wrong decisions, poor code — unfixed. Neglect accelerates deterioration. One broken window leads to a sense that nobody cares, which leads to more broken windows. Fix each one as you find it, or at minimum, board it up with a clear TODO and a plan.

title: Deploying Python Apps to Production
text:
# Deploying Python Apps to Production

Notes from shipping several Python services at work. The gap between "works on my machine" and "runs reliably in production" is wider than most developers expect.

## Containerization

Docker is the standard. Use multi-stage builds to keep images small — a build stage with full tooling and a runtime stage with only what the app needs.

```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY --from=builder /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages /usr/local/lib/python3.12/site-packages
COPY . /app
CMD ["python", "-m", "app.main"]
```

Pin exact dependency versions in production. `pip freeze` into a requirements file, not version ranges.

## CI/CD Pipelines

Automate everything: lint, test, build, deploy. A typical pipeline for a Python service:

1. Run `ruff` for linting and formatting checks
2. Run `pytest` with coverage thresholds
3. Build Docker image and push to registry
4. Deploy to staging environment
5. Run smoke tests against staging
6. Promote to production with rolling update

GitHub Actions works well for most teams. The key is making the pipeline fast — under ten minutes from push to production. Slow pipelines encourage developers to batch changes, which increases risk.

## Monitoring and Observability

At minimum: structured logging (JSON to stdout), health check endpoint, and error tracking (Sentry). For services with meaningful traffic, add metrics (Prometheus/Datadog) and distributed tracing.

Set up alerts for error rate spikes and latency percentile changes. Dashboard watching is not monitoring — you need automated alerts that page someone.

title: Database Migration Strategies
text:
# Database Migration Strategies

Managing schema changes in production databases without downtime. This has bitten me enough times that I now have a checklist I follow religiously.

## Zero-Downtime Deployment Pattern

The fundamental rule: never make a breaking schema change in a single deployment. Instead, use the expand-contract pattern:

1. **Expand:** Add the new column/table alongside the old one. Deploy code that writes to both.
2. **Migrate:** Backfill existing data from old to new structure.
3. **Contract:** Remove the old column/table. Deploy code that only uses the new structure.

Each step is a separate deployment. If anything goes wrong, you can roll back to the previous step without data loss.

## Migration Tools

Alembic for SQLAlchemy projects. Always auto-generate migrations then review them manually — the auto-generator misses renamed columns (it sees a drop and an add instead). Write both `upgrade()` and `downgrade()` functions for every migration.

## Rollback Plans

Every migration should have a tested rollback procedure. Before running a migration in production:

1. Run it against a copy of production data
2. Verify the rollback works cleanly
3. Time the migration — long-running ALTER TABLE operations can lock tables
4. Schedule during low-traffic periods if the migration involves table locks

## Common Pitfalls

- Adding a NOT NULL column without a default value breaks existing rows
- Renaming columns breaks any code that references the old name
- Large table ALTERs can lock the table for minutes or hours
- Foreign key additions on large tables can be extremely slow

The safest approach is always: make the change additive, deploy, verify, then clean up the old structure.

title: Debugging Memory Leaks
text:
# Debugging Memory Leaks

A systematic approach to finding and fixing memory leaks in Python applications. Most Python memory issues are not true leaks but rather unintentional object retention.

## Symptoms

- RSS (Resident Set Size) grows steadily over time
- Application becomes sluggish after running for hours or days
- OOM (Out of Memory) kills in container environments

## Profiling Tools

### tracemalloc (Built-in)

Python's built-in memory tracer. Take snapshots at intervals and compare:

```python
import tracemalloc
tracemalloc.start()
# ... run your code ...
snapshot = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
top_stats = snapshot.statistics('lineno')
for stat in top_stats[:10]:
    print(stat)
```

### objgraph

Visualize object reference graphs. Particularly useful for finding reference cycles:

```python
import objgraph
objgraph.show_most_common_types(limit=20)
objgraph.show_growth(limit=10)  # What's growing between calls?
```

### py-spy and memray

External profilers that attach to running processes without code modification. memray from Bloomberg is excellent for production memory analysis.

## Common Causes in Python

- **Caches without eviction:** Dictionaries used as caches that grow without bound. Use `functools.lru_cache` with a `maxsize` or a TTL-based cache.
- **Circular references:** Objects that reference each other prevent garbage collection of the entire cycle. The cyclic garbage collector handles most cases but can be slow with large cycles.
- **Global state accumulation:** Appending to module-level lists or dicts. Logging handlers that accumulate in long-running services.
- **Event listener leaks:** Registering callbacks without deregistering them. Common in GUI and async frameworks.

## Resolution Process

1. Reproduce the leak in a controlled environment
2. Identify the growing object type
3. Trace references back to the root cause
4. Fix the retention path
5. Verify with sustained load testing

title: API Design Best Practices
text:
# API Design Best Practices

Notes from designing and maintaining several REST APIs. Good interface design makes the difference between an API that developers love and one they tolerate.

## REST Conventions

Use nouns for resource endpoints, HTTP verbs for actions:
- `GET /users` — list users
- `POST /users` — create a user
- `GET /users/{id}` — retrieve a specific user
- `PUT /users/{id}` — replace a user
- `PATCH /users/{id}` — partially update a user
- `DELETE /users/{id}` — remove a user

Nest resources to express relationships: `GET /users/{id}/orders` lists orders for a specific user.

## Versioning

URL-based versioning (`/v1/users`) is the most explicit and easiest to manage. Header-based versioning is technically cleaner but harder for developers to discover and test.

Rule of thumb: version when you need to make breaking changes. Non-breaking additions (new optional fields, new endpoints) do not require a version bump.

## Error Handling

Return consistent error response structures. Every error should include:
- HTTP status code (in the response, not just the header)
- Machine-readable error code (e.g., `INVALID_EMAIL_FORMAT`)
- Human-readable message
- Optional: field-level validation details for 400 errors

## Documentation

OpenAPI (Swagger) specification as the source of truth. Generate docs from the spec, not the other way around. Include example requests and responses for every endpoint.

The best API documentation includes a quick-start guide that gets developers from zero to their first successful API call in under five minutes.

title: Code Review Checklist
text:
# Code Review Checklist

A systematic approach to reviewing pull requests. Quality reviews catch bugs and improve design — but they also teach and build shared understanding across the team.

## What to Look For

### Correctness

- Does the code actually solve the stated problem?
- Are edge cases handled? Empty inputs, null values, concurrent access.
- Are error conditions caught and handled appropriately?

### Readability

- Can you understand what the code does without reading the PR description?
- Are variable and function names descriptive and consistent?
- Is the code self-documenting, or does it need comments to explain non-obvious logic?

### Testing Coverage

- Are there tests for the new behavior?
- Do the tests cover both happy path and failure scenarios?
- Are the tests readable — can you understand what they verify without tracing through the implementation?

### Security Considerations

- Is user input validated and sanitized?
- Are credentials or secrets kept out of the code?
- Does the change introduce any new attack surfaces (SQL injection, XSS, SSRF)?

### Performance

- Are there any O(n^2) or worse algorithms hiding in loops?
- Database queries inside loops (N+1 problem)?
- Large allocations or unnecessary data copying?

## How to Give Feedback

Distinguish between blocking issues (must fix before merge) and suggestions (nice to have, author's choice). Use prefixes: "nit:" for style nitpicks, "question:" for things you want to understand, and no prefix for required changes.

Focus feedback on the code, not the author. "This function does too many things" is better than "You wrote a confusing function."

title: Weekly Reflection - January 15
text:
# Weekly Reflection - January 15

## What Went Well

Started tracking my expenses more carefully this week. Set up a simple spreadsheet to monitor where my money goes — turns out I have been spending way more on takeout than I realized. Almost forty dollars just on delivery fees in a single week.

Cooked dinner at home four out of five weeknights. The meal prep approach from Sunday is really paying off. Having containers ready in the fridge eliminates the temptation to order in when I am tired after work.

## What Needs Improvement

Reading goal is behind schedule. Aimed for two books per month but have not finished a single one in January. The issue is not time — it is that I default to scrolling my phone instead of picking up the book. Need to apply the environment design principle: put the book on the nightstand, charge the phone in a different room.

## Goals for Next Week

1. Continue cooking at home — target five out of five weeknights
2. Finish reading "Deep Work" (halfway through, should be doable)
3. Set up automatic transfer to savings account
4. Start the garden planning — research raised bed dimensions and soil mix

## Financial Snapshot

- Groceries: $62
- Eating out: $28
- Coffee shops: $18
- Transport: $45
- Subscriptions: $35

Total discretionary spending is down about fifteen percent compared to last week. The cooking habit is the biggest single factor.

title: App Idea: Recipe Ingredient Tracker
text:
# App Idea: Recipe Ingredient Tracker

A mobile app that manages pantry inventory and automatically generates shopping lists based on planned recipes for the week.

## Problem

I frequently buy ingredients I already have at home, or I get to the store and cannot remember what I need. The friction of manually checking the pantry before shopping leads to waste and redundant purchases.

## Core Features

### Pantry Management

- Scan barcodes or manually add items
- Track quantities and expiration dates
- Alert when items are running low or about to expire
- Categorize by location (fridge, freezer, pantry shelves)

### Recipe Integration

- Import recipes from URLs or manual entry
- Cross-reference recipe ingredients against current pantry
- Highlight what you already have and what you need to buy
- Scale recipes up or down and adjust shopping list accordingly

### Smart Shopping List

- Auto-generated from selected recipes minus pantry stock
- Organized by store section (produce, dairy, canned goods)
- Shareable with household members
- Price estimation based on historical purchases

## Technical Approach

React Native for cross-platform mobile. SQLite for local pantry database — no cloud dependency, data stays on device. Optional sync via iCloud or Google Drive for household sharing.

Barcode scanning via the phone camera using an open-source UPC database. Recipe import would use a simple HTML parser to extract structured ingredient lists from popular recipe sites.

## Monetization

Freemium model: free for personal use with basic features. Premium tier adds household sharing, price tracking, and meal planning calendar. No ads ever.

title: Learning Rust - Week 3
text:
# Learning Rust - Week 3

Getting into the ownership model now. This is where Rust diverges most dramatically from Python and other garbage-collected languages.

## Ownership Rules

Three rules that the compiler enforces at compile time:
1. Each value in Rust has exactly one owner
2. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped
3. You can have either one mutable reference OR any number of immutable references (not both)

This eliminates data races at compile time. No garbage collector needed — memory is freed deterministically when the owner goes out of scope.

## The Borrow Checker

The borrow checker enforces the ownership rules. It analyzes lifetimes to ensure references never outlive the data they point to. Coming from Python where everything is a reference and the GC handles cleanup, this feels restrictive at first.

But the mental model clicks after a while: you are telling the compiler your intent, and it verifies that your intent is safe. In Python, you discover these bugs at runtime (or never, if the race condition is rare). In Rust, the compiler catches them before the code runs.

## Comparing to Python

| Concept | Python | Rust |
|---------|--------|------|
| Memory management | Garbage collection | Ownership + borrowing |
| Null values | None (runtime errors) | Option<T> (compile-time) |
| Error handling | Exceptions | Result<T, E> (must handle) |
| Concurrency | GIL limits true parallelism | Fearless concurrency via ownership |
| Speed | Interpreted, ~100x slower | Compiled, near C speed |

## This Week's Exercise

Built a simple CLI tool that counts word frequencies in a text file. Ran into borrow checker issues when trying to sort a HashMap by value — had to collect into a Vec of tuples first. The error messages were actually helpful once I learned to read them.

title: Home Office Ergonomics
text:
# Home Office Ergonomics

After developing wrist pain from my temporary pandemic desk setup, I invested time researching proper ergonomics for a productive workspace.

## Desk and Chair

The desk surface should be at elbow height when seated with feet flat on the floor. For me that is 28 inches. A sit-stand desk is ideal — alternating between sitting and standing throughout the day reduces back strain.

Chair: invest in a quality ergonomic chair with adjustable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrest height. The Herman Miller Aeron and Steelcase Leap are the standards for a reason. Budget option: a good task chair plus a separate lumbar pillow.

## Monitor Positioning

Top of the screen should be at or slightly below eye level. Distance: arm's length (about 20-26 inches). If using dual monitors, angle them in a shallow V with the primary monitor directly in front.

For laptop-only setups, a laptop stand plus external keyboard and mouse is essential. Looking down at a laptop screen for eight hours creates chronic neck strain.

## Keyboard and Mouse

Split or ergonomic keyboards reduce ulnar deviation — the lateral bending of the wrists that causes strain. I use a Kinesis Advantage360 which took two weeks to adjust to but eliminated my wrist pain completely.

Mouse alternatives: vertical mouse (Logitech MX Vertical) or trackball (Kensington SlimBlade). Both keep the wrist in a more natural position than a traditional mouse.

## Breaks and Movement

The 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Get up and move for five minutes every hour. Stretch wrists, shoulders, and neck regularly.

title: Garden Project Planning
text:
# Garden Project Planning

Planning to build raised beds in the backyard this spring. This will be a weekend project spread across several weeks.

## Raised Bed Design

Target: three 4x8 foot beds, 12 inches deep. Cedar boards for rot resistance — untreated lumber only (no pressure-treated wood near food plants). Each bed needs about 32 cubic feet of soil mix.

Layout: orient beds north-south for maximum sun exposure. Leave 3-foot paths between beds for comfortable access with a wheelbarrow.

## Soil Mix

The standard raised bed formula:
- 40% topsoil
- 40% compost
- 20% aeration amendment (perlite or vermiculite)

Buy compost in bulk from a local landscape supplier — bagged compost from hardware stores is three to four times more expensive per cubic foot.

## Composting Setup

Starting a three-bin compost system alongside the raised beds. Greens (nitrogen): kitchen scraps, coffee grounds, fresh grass clippings. Browns (carbon): dried leaves, cardboard, straw. Maintain a roughly 3:1 brown-to-green ratio by volume.

Turn the pile every two to three weeks. Active composting produces usable compost in three to four months. Passive piles take six to twelve months but require less effort.

## Seasonal Planting Schedule

- **Early Spring (March):** Peas, lettuce, spinach, radishes — cold-tolerant crops
- **Late Spring (May):** Tomatoes, peppers, squash, beans — after last frost
- **Summer succession:** Plant new lettuce and radish rows every two weeks for continuous harvest
- **Fall (September):** Garlic, kale, overwintering onions

Keep a garden journal to track what works. Note planting dates, varieties, yields, and pest issues for each season.
